I'm now looking at the small arrow pattern of two 5s forming a diagonal pair, wondering if this represents a mini-shape whose orientation tells me where to place the marker relative to the target shape. Testing whether the marker sits at the continuation of that diagonal line doesn't match the actual marker position in ex1, so that theory seems to fail and I need another explanation for the offset.

Checking the other examples for consistency: in ex3 marker (10,4) continues the diagonal from the 5-shape, while in ex1 and ex2 the marker sits diagonally adjacent to a target shape cell instead. So the placement rule seems inconsistent between examples, and I need to figure out which pattern actually generalizes.

Perhaps the marker bounces off the 5-shapes themselves rather than the edge — checking the cells along the diagonal, they're all empty, so that's not it either, and the target (9,3) is far to the left, suggesting I'm misreading the direction entirely.

Testing the same line-trajectory idea on example 3 also fails to produce the right answer, so this reflection/line approach only coincidentally worked for example 1. I'm now reconsidering an adjacency-based rule instead, comparing how the marker sits relative to the vertical domino shape across examples, but the positioning seems inconsistent between example 1 and example 3, so maybe the real pattern is about the overall L-shaped or arrow-like geometry formed by the 5s and marker together.

Switching approach, I'm wondering if the marker's position mirrors the original 5-arrow's offset relative to some anchor shape — like the plus-shape in ex1 sits near the 3 at a specific offset from its center, and maybe the target domino should get the same relative offset to produce the new marker location. It's a rough match so far, not exact.

Let me check ex3 against this idea: the arrow's 5s at (8,2),(9,3) and marker 2 at (10,4), but the diagonal chain doesn't clearly connect to a nearby shape. Maybe instead the length of the 5-chain indicates how many diagonal steps the marker travels, meaning two steps rather than one.

Testing this: ex3's marker output at (2,8), and stepping down-left two from (4,10) or checking nearby shape cells like (3,7) reveals it's a shape cell adjacent diagonally to the marker. Same pattern holds for ex1 (marker at (9,16), shape found one step up-left at (8,15)) and ex2 (marker at (9,3), shape one step up-right at (8,4)) -- so in every example the marker ends up diagonally adjacent to a shape cell, just via different directions.

But when I check the actual arrow direction (ex1 goes from (12,13) to (14,11), a down-left path) versus the marker-to-shape relation (up-left), they don't match, so simple direction copying isn't the rule. I'm now wondering if instead the chosen shape cell is the "outer corner" tip of the shape furthest from its body -- for ex1's vertical domino at column 15, rows 7-8, that would pick out one of the four diagonal corners, matching (9,16).

For ex3, following the arrow from (10,4) through (8,2) continues to (7,1) then (6,0), reaching the edge -- but that doesn't match the (2,8) output, so I need to reconsider whether the arrow's extension is really what determines the target cell.

Ex2: tracing the same bounce pattern from (15,11), the path ricochets off the right wall, then the top wall, then heads toward the left wall.

Continuing the bounce, it goes down-right and stops at (9,3) where it hits a 9 — confirming the rule that balls bounce off walls and halt just before a shape cell, with 5s cleared from the grid. But I don't see the actual test input grid provided yet, so I don't have anything to apply this rule to — I need to see the test grid before I can make a prediction.

The colored cell travels along that diagonal (in the direction indicated by the 5s), reflecting off the grid walls, until it would run into a shape cell — it stops at the last free cell before the collision. The 5s and the original colored cell are erased, and the colored cell is drawn at its stopping position.
